purpose: Quinidine is used to treat certain types of irregular heartbeats, called arrhythmias, to help your heart beat in a normal, steady rhythm. It can also be used in some cases to treat a severe form of malaria. Your doctor prescribes it to help your heart work more efficiently and safely.
how_it_works: Your heart uses electrical signals to tell it when to beat. Quinidine works by slowing down those electrical signals in the heart muscle, which helps prevent the abnormal, chaotic beats that cause arrhythmias. Think of it like a traffic controller that keeps the electrical signals in your heart moving in an orderly way.
common_side_effects: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and stomach upset are very common, especially when you first start taking it. You may also experience dizziness, headache, or ringing in your ears (called tinnitus). Some people notice changes in vision or a mild skin rash.
warnings: Quinidine can sometimes cause serious heart rhythm problems in rare cases, so your doctor will monitor your heart with regular EKGs. Tell your doctor right away if you feel faint, have a very fast or pounding heartbeat, or feel unusually dizzy. Also let your doctor know about all other medicines you take, as quinidine can interact with many medications and may not be safe during pregnancy.
typical_dosing: Dosing varies depending on the condition being treated and the specific form of quinidine used. A typical adult dose might be 200–400 mg taken by mouth every 6 to 8 hours, but your doctor will customize the dose for you. Always take it exactly as prescribed and do not stop it suddenly without talking to your doctor first.
